neutral_facts.value: The accused, who was the brother of the deceased, was involved in a violent incident where the deceased suffered fatal injuries. The deceased had a history of alcohol addiction and had previously tormented, abused, and threatened the accused. On the night of the incident, the deceased consumed alcohol and told the accused to leave the house, warning that he would kill him if he did not. The accused, who had attempted suicide by holding live electrical wires, lost self-control due to the sudden and grave provocation from the deceased. The accused inflicted fatal injuries on the deceased using a pick-axe. The accused's actions were deemed to be a result of temporary loss of self-control rather than premeditation. The accused was initially convicted under s.302 IPC for murder, but the conviction was converted to s.304 Part I IPC under Exception 1 to s.300 IPC due to the provocation and loss of self-control. The accused was sentenced to imprisonment for 10 years, a fine of Rs. 1,000, or simple imprisonment for six months if the fine was not paid.

quotes.text: Partly allowing the appeal, the Court HELD:1.1. The conditions which have to be satisfied for invoking Exception 1 to the Section 300 were laid down by Supreme Court in K.M. Nanavati case as (a) the deceased must have given provocation to the accused; (b) the provocation must be grave; (c) the provocation must be sudden; (d) the offender, by the reason of the said provocation, should have been deprived of his power of self-control; (e) the offender should have killed the deceased during the continuance of the deprivation of power of self-control; and (f) the offender must have caused the death of the person who gave the provocation or the death of any other person by mistake or accident.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the appellant caused the death of his brother due to grave and sudden provocation, and that the deceased had a history of abusing and threatening the appellant. The deceased had consumed alcohol and told the appellant to leave the house, otherwise he would kill him, leading to a sudden loss of self-control by the appellant.

quotes.text: The prosecution does not dispute this position and in fact, has relied upon these facts to show motive.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the appellant's actions were a result of grave and sudden provocation, and that the deceased's abusive behavior over time led to a loss of self-control. The appellant had tried to commit suicide by holding live electrical wires, indicating a temporary loss of self-control rather than premeditation.

quotes.text: The defence of the appellant in his statement under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 19735 that some third person had killed his brother Dashrath Nirmalkar, carries no weight and has been rightly rejected.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle of Exception 1 to Section 300 of the IPC, which recognizes that culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation or another person by mistake or accident.
